catalog_locator: Sec. 2.3 'Phonological variations', printed p. 11 (PDF p. 11 of 28), the two paragraphs after the vowel chart; Chart F, p. 12; Appendix B 'Wordlists', Dambi rows, pp. 16-27 (forms cited here from pp. 16-18)
catalog_quote: There seems to be a closer correspondence of vowels between Patep and Kumalu-Dambi-Mumengtein, even though they don't share as many cognates overall. Initial unstressed syllables in Patep always have the vowel schwa [ə]. It appears to be a neutralised vowel, since some of the other dialects have full vowels in that position. A further difference is that for some words, Kumalu, Mumengtein, and Pelenkwa have a different stress pattern, so that not only does the initial syllable have a full vowel, but it also receives stress. Chart F shows other phonological comparisons between the various dialects.
world_status: accessible description is silent on stress

Courtesy a full-text search for stress/accent the other copies we hold under the same glottocode directory (Hooley 1976, McElhanon 1984) finds no stress/accent hits; Adams & Lauck 1985 (already recorded) has its Patep/Kumalu/Mumengtein/Pelenkwa stress lines at the text layerand does not name Dambi. No new works added.

sources.note: No rule for Dambi. Sec. 2.3 'Phonological variations' (p. 11): 'Initial unstressed syllables in Patep always have the vowel schwa.. for some words, Kumalu, Mumengtein, and Pelenkwa have a different stress pattern, so that not only does the initial syllable have a full vowel, but it also receives stress.' Dambi is not named in the stress remark. Chart F (p. 12) gives Dambi segmental traits only. Appendix B (pp. 16-27) prints a stress-marked Dambi (Zoo village) wordlist row (e.g. lu ka'nsEk 'head', 'mEnik 'bird', ka'ndik, ba'linek, 'manon) without any statement.
